paper_title: GPBam: A Retrieval-Aware German Public Law Exam Benchmark

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Legal reasoning in civil-law systems is not rule-lookup: the German state examination asks for a structured opinion (Gutachten) that names the governing norms, applies them to the facts, and argues to a conclusion. We introduce GPBam (German Public Law Bar-style Exam), 81 public-law examination cases with reference solutions, paired with a recitation task over 200 statutory provisions. Drawn from state examination preparation, the cases are broad and rarely repeat, and are not publicly available - we find no evidence of exact-solution memorisation in the models we evaluate, and keeping them private limits contamination. Because each reference solution's cited norms form a retrieval gold set over the very instances the essays are graded on, GPBam scores retrieval and long-form generation jointly, which makes it a benchmark for legal retrieval as well as for legal writing and lets us ask how much retrieval quality a legal opinion actually needs. Across 32 open-weight and proprietary models evaluated without retrieval, scores span 4.81-76.42 out of 100. Supplying the law helps modestly: across seven models and eight retrieval configurations, retrieval performance varies nearly threefold and buys at most 4.1 essay points, and nothing significant for three of the seven, while an oracle with 91% gold-norm recall improves scores by 2-6 points. Essay quality strongly tracks prior knowledge: verbatim statute recall, measured in a separate task, correlates at $ρ= 0.92$ over 32 models.

sections.content: GPBam: Retrieval-Aware German Public Law Exam Benchmark1 Abdullah Al ZUBAER a,2, Lorenz WENDLINGER b, Simon Alexander NONN a, Michael GRANITZER and Jelena MITROVIĆ Universität Passau, Passau, Germany Technische Hochschule Deggendorf, Deggendorf, Germany Abstract. Legal reasoning in civil-law systems is not rule-lookup: the German state examination asks for structured opinion (Gutachten) that names the governing norms, applies them to the facts, and argues to conclusion. We introduce GPBam (German Public Law Bar-style Exam), 81 public-law examination cases with reference solutions, paired with recitation task over 200 statutory provisions. Drawn from state examination preparation, the cases are broad and rarely repeat, and are not publicly available - we find no evidence of exact-solution memorisation in the models we evaluate, and keeping them private limits contamination. Because each reference solutions cited norms form retrieval gold set over the very instances the essays are graded on, GPBam scores retrieval and long-form generation jointly, which makes it benchmark for legal retrieval as well as for legal writing and lets us ask how much retrieval quality legal opinion actually needs. Across 32 open-weight and proprietary models evaluated without retrieval, scores span 4.81 76.42 out of 100. Supplying the law helps modestly: across seven models and eight retrieval configurations, retrieval performance varies nearly threefold and buys at most 4.1 essay points, and nothing significant for three of the seven, while an oracle with 91% gold-norm recall improves scores by 26 points. Essay quality strongly tracks prior knowledge: verbatim statute recall, measured in separate task, correlates at ρ=0.92 over 32 models. Keywords. Legal NLP, German Public Law, Legal Retrieval Benchmark, Large Language Models, Retrieval-Augmented Generation 1. Introduction Many established legal benchmarks use classification, multiple-choice, or shortanswer formats [1,2,3]. This permits standardized automatic scoring, but does not represent how case-based tasks in German legal education and the First State 1This paper is an extended version of paper accepted at the 39th International Conference on Legal Knowledge and Information Systems (JURIX 2026). 2Corresponding Author, abdullahal.zubaer@uni-passau.de. These authors contributed equally to this work. Examination assess legal reasoning. typical case task requires complete legal opinion (Gutachten): identify the issues and governing norms, state the requirements of each norm, apply them to the facts, and reach conclusion. The same structure recurs over the issues and sub-issues of the case. correct final conclusion can therefore conceal missing or incorrect intermediate analysis, which labelbased benchmarks do not measure directly [1,2,3]. Evaluating the full reasoning document is necessary for this examination setting [4]. Several recent benchmarks include open-ended legal tasks. GreekBarBench asks questions from five areas of the Greek bar examination, supplies chapterlevel statutory context, and requires citations to both articles and case facts [5]. LEXam contains 2,841 open-ended questions from law examinations and accompanies them with guidance on the expected reasoning approach [6]. For German law, BenGER evaluates complete exam-style case solutions alongside short doctrinal tasks, but disables retrieval and tool-use endpoints for the evaluated systems [4]. Retrieval-focused benchmarks address different stage: LegalBenchRAG measures whether system locates the relevant spans, not whether those spans improve complete legal opinion [7]. These benchmarks therefore emphasize different stages of legal problem solving. Their complementary designs motivate evaluating statutory recall, retrieval, and downstream use within the same document-level task. We introduce GPBam (German Public Law Bar-style Exam), benchmark that scores statute retrieval and long-form legal writing on the same 81 stateexam-style public-law cases, drawn from the University of Passaus State Examination Preparation Course in Public Law. Each case pairs fact pattern (Sachverhalt) with an extensively reasoned reference solution. The task is documentlevel: model receives the case and writes complete German legal opinion (Gutachten), including table of contents and an assessment of every question raised. The reference solutions average 7,080 words, compared with 924 for the case facts, and contain substantially more statutory references. This asymmetry is part of the task: the model must determine much of the governing law rather than extract it from the question. The cases are also broad and rarely repeat: the topics their authors label are mostly unique to single case, and one case raises median of eight of them across median of twelve law books. Keeping the cases and reference solutions non-public also reduces the risk that they enter modeltraining corpora and contaminate the evaluation [8]. direct text-overlap analysis finds no evidence of exact-solution memorisation of the reference solutions (Section 3.2). GPBam evaluates statutory access in two complementary ways. First, the Essay Writing task is run without retrieval and with statutory context retrieved from federal and Bavarian statutes. We compare retrieval strategies and context budgets, and include an oracle condition that supplies the statutes cited by the reference solution, separating retrieval failure from failure to use relevant provisions. Second, Article Recitation names provision and asks the model to reproduce its text. The task covers 200 provisions: 100 frequently cited by the GPBam reference solutions and 100 frequently cited by German courts. It removes issue spotting and subsumption, providing separate measure of closed-book statutory-text recall. Essays are scored against the reference solution by three open-weight judges; we take their per-case median and separately measure the overlap of statutory citations. Across 32 models evaluated without retrieval, essay scores span 4.8176.42 points on the 0100 scale. Calibration controls anchor the scale empirically: the reference solutions score 100, whereas wrong-case solutions and fact-pattern echoes score 0. Essay score correlates with Article Recitation on the GPBam provisions at ρ=0.92, while correlation with citation overlap, measured against the reference solution, is ρ=0.94. Supplying statutes via retrieval system has limited effect in the present setup. Across the tested retrieval configurations, gold-norm recall rises nearly threefold, from 3.50% to 9.61% at k=10 and from 8.52% to 23.92% at k=50, while the largest non-oracle improvement over no retrieval is 4.1 essay score points, and for three out of seven generators no configuration improves significantly on no retrieval at all. The oracle, which supplies the statutes the reference solution cites and reaches 91.31% recall, raises essay scores by 26 points and does so for every one of the seven evaluated models. These results do not show that statutory knowledge causes higher essay scores. They do show that supplying statutory text under the tested conditions does not close the observed performance gap, while closed-book statutory recall covaries strongly with essay quality. Our contributions are the following: We introduce GPBam, 81 German state-exam-style public-law cases with reference solutions, formulated as complete legal-opinion writing rather than classification or short-answer prediction, and held out rather than published: we find no evidence of exact-solution memorisation of the reference solutions in any evaluated model, and keeping the material private limits contamination. Because each reference solutions cited norms form retrieval gold set over the same 81 instances the essays are scored on, GPBam measures retrieval and long-form generation jointly. This is what lets us ask how much retrieval quality legal essay actually needs, and it makes the benchmark usable for legal retrieval independently of the essay task. We pair the essay task with Article Recitation over 200 provisions, making statutory recall observable separately from issue spotting, subsumption, and legal writing. We report 32-model no-retrieval study using three-judge ensemble, citation overlap, together with an analysis of inter-judge agreement. We evaluate statute retrieval for complete opinions across seven models, with controlled changes to retrieval method, corpus, and context budget, and an oracle upper bound using the reference solutions cited statutes. Findings show that supplying statutes helps modestly: nearly threefold spread in gold-norm recall is worth at most 4.1 points of essay score, with no significant gain for three of the seven generators, while an oracle at 91.31% recall raises every generator by 26 points. 2. Related Work 2.1. From Legal Understanding to Open-Ended Examination Tasks Many early legal NLP benchmarks framed the domain as classification, multiplechoice, or other short/task-specific outputs. LexGLUE groups document and clause classification tasks [1], LegalBench assembles hand-built tasks around common-law reasoning [2], and LawBench organises Chinese legal tasks into memorisation, understanding and application [3]. Their evaluations are often outcomefocused, so model can be credited for correct answer reached by faulty reasoning. Prompting general LLM on legal argument mining task did not by itself dissolve these tasks [9]. Nearer to the present setting, open-weight LLMs have been put to range of German legal-education tasks, where capability falls away as the material turns doctrinal: labelling the components of Gutachtenstil, and working over whole legal opinions rather than short spans. On those two, neither longer context window nor prompt engineering carried the models past bag-of-words baseline [10]. Recent benchmarks increasingly include open-ended examination tasks. Outside law, SciEx grades free-text exam answers with both human experts and automatic graders [11]. Within law, oab-bench draws 105 questions from the Brazilian bar examination and applies the official grading guidelines through an LLM judge [12]. GreekBarBench covers five areas of the Greek bar and requires citations to statutory articles and to case facts, scored on three dimensions [5]. LEXam derives 7,537 questions from 340 Swiss law exams, 2,841 of them openended. Each open question is paired with reference answer and reasoning approach expected [6]. PLawBench and JurisBench extend the setting to professional practice in Chinese law, the former with expert-written rubric items across 13 scenarios [13], the latter through multi-stage litigation workflow in which errors cascade [14]. Surveys of the area report the same trajectory [15]. Two properties separate this line of work from GPBam. The first is the unit of evaluation. LEXam, PLawBench and JurisBench score answers to individual questions or workflow stages, and GreekBarBench scores one answer to case-specific question against span-based rubrics. GPBam scores one complete Gutachten per case: table of contents followed by full assessment that answers every question raised in the Sachverhalt, with no study-imposed outputtoken cap. The reference solutions are correspondingly long, at 7,080 words on average against 924 for the facts - roughly twenty-nine times the 247-word mean reference answer of LEXam [6], whose open questions are individually scorable sub-problems rather than whole opinions. GreekBarBench scores one answer per question against expert-annotated spans for facts, cited articles and analysis [5], so its unit is passage within an answer. The biggest difference is jurisdiction. Common-law and Chinese material dominates, while civil-law systems, in which the analysis is anchored in codified statutes rather than precedent, are less well covered [6]. For German law, employment-contract clauses have been classified as valid, unfair or void [16], which isolates subsumption at clause level. Among the benchmarks reviewed, BenGER is the closest work to ours. It evaluates 596 exam-style cases spanning civil, criminal, and public law and multiple stages of legal education, together with 531 shorter doctrinal items. Its judge scores ten weighted dimensions and is checked against three independent blind human gradings on controlled subset [4]. Retrieval and tool-use endpoints are switched off throughout, so its systems answer from parametric knowledge alone. GPBam is narrower - 81 state-exam-style public-law cases from single stateexamination preparation course - and uses that depth for two things BenGER does not measure: what happens when the statutes are supplied via retrieval, and how much of the statutory text models retain without external knowledge analogues to closed-book performance. 2.2. Legal Context and LLM-Based Evaluation Supplying legal context. Retrieval augmentation conditions generation on passages fetched at inference time [17], and the pipelines now in use extend that basic loop on both sides of the retriever - rewriting or diversifying the query before search [18,19], fusing dense and lexical channel [20,21], and re-ranking the pool before it reaches the generator - family the surveys group as advanced and modular RAG [22]. Our retrieval ladder walks exactly these components over statutory law. The central question, however, is not only whether these techniques retrieve more relevant legal material, but whether those retrieval gains improve the models final answers. relationship that legal RAG evaluations have only recently begun to examine directly. Much of the existing legal literature evaluates retrieval separately from generation. LegalBench-RAG, for example, scores the retrieval step alone [7]. Pairing statutory corpus with labour-law benchmark puts retrieval-augmented accuracy well below the claims made for it [23]. An evaluation of three commercial legal research tools built on retrieval measures hallucination rates between 17% and 33% [24]. Varying the German legal context supplied to the model shows that full-text sources help only moderately, while distilled examination guidelines help more [16]. Context length can reduce performance even under perfect retrieval and when irrelevant tokens are masked [25]. Where retrieval and downstream answering are evaluated jointly, better access to relevant legal context does not necessarily yield better answers. In Bar Exam QA, which uses short, stylized fact patterns with four answer choices, and Housing Statute QA, which uses binary yes/no questions, structured legal-reasoning query expansion improves recall for several retrievers, but these gains do not consistently translate into higher answer accuracy [26]. These studies therefore either evaluate retrieval in isolation or measure its downstream effect on question-answering or classification tasks. None of the reviewed studies examines whether retrieved statutory text improves complete examination essay in civil-law system. GPBam runs the same 81 cases with and without retrieval and adds an oracle condition that supplies the statutes cited by the reference solution, which separates retrieval cannot find the norms from the norms do not help. Probing statutory knowledge directly. parallel line measures whether models hold statutory text at all. LawBench includes memorisation level [3]; CLaw segments 306 Chinese national statutes to subparagraph level and reports that models struggle to reproduce provisions faithfully [27]; LeKUBE evaluates statute recitation and recall under knowledge updates [28]. GPBam adopts the same idea as separate closed-book task over 200 provisions, and then correlates it with essay quality across models. This is what lets us ask whether the bottleneck on Gutachten is knowing the law or applying it. LLM judges. Judging long-form legal answers at benchmark scale is constrained by the cost of expert annotation: it is slow, requires specialised lawyers, and does not scale to the number of models and conditions benchmark must cover [5,29]. The expert grades themselves are also noisy. Where the same law-exam answers have been regraded by many markers, the harshest and the most generous mark on one answer differ by 6.47 points on average, on scale that runs from 0 to 18 [30,4]. This variability cautions against treating one markers grade as definitive ground truth. Lexical overlap with reference solution is no substitute [6], because legally equivalent analyses differ in wording. Recent benchmarks therefore grade with LLM judges [31,5,6,4]. Reported failure modes include self-preference, where an evaluator favours its own generations [32], and sensitivity to prompt [33]. Benchmarks respond by validating the judge: GreekBarBench builds meta-evaluation set and finds that span-based rubrics improve alignment [5]; LEXam uses judge ensemble with expert validation [6]; BenGER benchmarks its judge against pool of human markers, obtaining r=0.76 under Pearson and κ=0.60 [4]; oab-bench reports strong correlation between frontier judge and human examiners [12]. parallel line changes the unit of assessment instead of validating holistic one: LeMAJ splits legal answer into small, individually checkable units it calls legal data points, and scores those without consulting reference answer [29], and DeCE separates precision from recall against criteria extracted from the gold answer, reporting correlation with expert judgement of r=0.78 on legal questionanswering task with citation grounding, against r=0.35 for pointwise scoring [34]. For German exam scripts in particular, comparison of 27 models against examiner marks under quadratic weighted kappa finds that pooling several models tracks the examiners more closely than any single model does, by as much as 0.15 kappa [35]. Within GradeLegals two datasets, agreement was far higher on public-law scripts than on criminal-law ones, so the domain GPBam covers is the one where automatic marking has so far proved most tractable. GPBam scores each essay against the reference solution with three open-weight judges and takes the per-case median. We report inter-judge agreement at essay and model level and report fitted adjustment for judge-generator self-preference. 3. The GPBam Benchmark 3.1. Examination Setting German public-law examination cases present fact pattern and one or more questions whose solution often requires procedural and substantive legal analysis. The expected solution is not list of rules but structured legal opinion (Gutachten). Following the legal opinion style (Gutachtenstil ), the reasoning typically proceeds through four components: an Obersatz identifying the legal issue to be examined, Definition specifying the relevant legal requirements, the Subsumtion of the facts under those requirements, and an Ergebnis stating the resulting conclusion. This structure recurs across relevant issues and sub-issues in the solution, making the appropriate unit of evaluation an entire reasoning document rather than an isolated answer span. The source documents of GPBam belong to the Examenskurs im Öffentlichen Recht (State Examination Preparation Course in Public Law) of the University of Passaus Institute for Legal Didactics. They are practice examination written at the level and in the format of the German state examination. We therefore use state-exam style rather than treating the documents as official stateexamination papers. Each case fact pattern is accompanied by an extensively reasoned model solution that serves as the reference solution for the respective case. 3.2. Dataset Construction and Characteristics GPBam comprises 81 German public-law examination cases sourced from Examenskurs im Öffentlichen Recht (State Examination Preparation Course in Public Law) of the University of Passaus Institute for Legal Didactics. Each case pairs Sachverhalt, factual scenario followed by the questions the examinee must answer, with Lösung, reference solution that develops the expected legal analysis in full. Length. Table 1 summarizes the corpus. The two components are strongly asymmetric: reference solutions are around 8 longer than case facts in words (7080 vs. 924) and in tokens (13855 vs. 1657). The task is therefore long-form generation, rather than the short-answer and multiple-choice formats of many widely used legal benchmarks [2,1], placing it alongside with recent free-text legal benchmarks [6,5]. Length alone understates the difficulty. Case facts cite almost no law (44 unique statutory references), whereas the corresponding reference solutions cite 5216. This gap characterises the core challenge: models must identify the governing law themselves rather than apply law supplied to them. It motivates both experimental conditions: supplying the relevant statutes through retrieval (Section 3.5), and probing statutory knowledge directly through article recitation (Section 3.3.2). Topical coverage. The cases are written as preparation for the state examination, therefore they are set to span the examinable material rather than to focus on one doctrine. Each reference solution closes with list of the topics its case examines, compiled by the course authors; 80 of the 81 solutions carry one. These lists name 520 distinct topics, of which 83% appear in exactly one case, and the most frequent of them, the Anfechtungsklage (action for annulment), in 13. single case raises median of eight topics and cites median of twelve distinct law books, so breadth is property of the individual case and not only of the collection. Contamination analysis. case whose solution model had already read would be answered from memory rather than from reasoning. We probe this on the essays directly: for each, we measure the longest exact word-span it shares with its own reference solution, and the same quantity against four other control cases solutions, which share the genre, the Gutachtenstil conventions and much statutory wording but nothing case-specific. Memorisation of Lösung would show as spans of dozens to hundreds of words above that control; it does not appear. The median longest match is 7 words against cases own solution and 5 against the controls, an excess of two; the longest raw match is 38 words and the largest excess over control 34, with only five essays at twenty or above. Per-model median excess ranges from one to three words across all 32 generators, including the two highest-scoring systems, whose longer raw matches are offset by equally longer control matches. All five are quoted source material rather than recalled analysis - the question posed in the Sachverhalt, passages of statutes, and court passage that essay and solution both cite. The test only bounds the strongest exposure, to the exact reference solutions, but does not test for paraphrases or the Sachverhalt alone. 3.3. Benchmark Tasks Figure 1 summarizes the GPBam benchmark tasks, which separates integrated legal writing from statutory recall and consists of two distinct but related tasks: (1) full legal essay writing and (2) article recitation. Essay writing uses 81 case/solution pairs of Section 3.2 and is run in two context conditions, without and with retrieved context; besides that context, the two conditions also differ in the framing of the instruction (Section 3.3.1). Article recitation uses two fixed sets of 100 provisions, involves no fact pattern, and is scored against official statutory text. The first task measures what model produces when the applicable law has to be identified and applied. The second measures how accurately it reproduces statutory wording when the provision is named for it. Table 2 provides further details. 3.3.1. Full Legal Essay Writing Task. The input is the case facts to the model and the expected output is the complete legal opinion in German that answers every question raised in the case facts. The reference solution is withheld during generation and is never part of the models input, it serves as the evaluation target used by the judge ensemble (Section 3.7, Section 3.8). Instruction. All 81 cases are inserted into German instruction template with two slots, context and case text. The template describes the input as stateexamination-level case to be answered within four hours and asks for table of contents followed by complete legal assessment. It requires citations to identify the paragraph (Abs.), sentence (S.), number (Nr.), or letter (Buchst.) of provision where applicable, and instructs the model to avoid unspecific references. The prompt specifies no output-length limit. No-RAG and Law-RAG use variants of the same template, with the differences described under Conditions below. See the complete prompts in Appendix A.2.1 and A.2.2. In No-RAG the context slot is empty, so the case facts are the only Conditions. case-specific input. In Law-RAG the slot holds <context> block containing the retrieved provisions, each wrapped in <norm> element that carries its citation, its jurisdiction and its heading as attributes, so that the model can cite the provision rather than its position in the list. The case text is identical across the two conditions, but the instruction is not. The Law-RAG template adds guidance on how to read the retrieved material: that the selection is incomplete and partly irrelevant, that state law may be missing from it even where it governs, that provisions absence from the block is not evidence that it does not apply, and that the essay should cite the applicable norms whether or not their text is printed. It also drops three No-RAG-only sentences, including an instruction to cite exclusively from the considerations the model has identified. The two conditions therefore differ in access to statutory text and in the instruction that frames it, which is confound to keep in view when reading any No-RAGLaw-RAG difference. 3.3.2. Article Recitation Task. Article Recitation asks model to reproduce single statutory provision from its identifier alone. The input is law book and number, as stored in the respective set. The expected output is the text of that provision. The German prompt requests the exact wording of the current version, without warnings, an introduction, or follow-up questions, and the most detailed available summary if exact reproduction is not possible. The generated text is compared with the stored official text of the provision using ROUGE-L F1 (Section 3.8). No case facts, retrieval, or reference solution are involved in this task. See the complete prompt in Section A.2.3. Provision sets. provision is named the way German lawyer cites one: by the law book it sits in - the statute, such as the Verwaltungsgerichtsordnung (VwGO) - and its number within that statute. Each of the two sets holds 100 such provisions. Figure 1. The two GPBam tasks and their data. Benchmark Records and Access Both halves of the law corpus are pinned: federal law to gesetze-im-internet revision 67e05675, scrape dated 2026-02-09 that parses to 106,354 provisions across 5,936 law books, and Bavarian state law to crawl of BAYERN.RECHTs statute index taken on 2026-08-31, giving 7,008 articles from 720 statutes. The cases and reference solutions are teaching material of the Institute for Legal Didactics. Most are based on original state-examination papers, which places them under copyright, and they remain in active use in the examination course they were written for. They are therefore not redistributed. GPBam is held-out benchmark: we evaluate on it and release raw scores, but not the underlying documents or generations. Scores, code and the retrieval task (query rewrites, statute corpus) are released at https://github.com/wendli01/gpbam 3.4. Model Selection Table 3 shows the models used in our experiments. We selected heterogeneous candidate pool to cover dimensions plausibly related to long-form legal performance: capability, parameter scale, architecture, training objective, developer family, and deployment regime. This breadth reduces the risk that the benchmark findings reflects one model family or configuration. Because complete legal opinion requires sustained, multi-step analysis, we include both standard instruction-tuned and explicitly reasoning-oriented models rather than restricting the evaluation to one inference paradigm. We likewise include proprietary hosted systems and open-weight models. The later permit on-premise deployment and processing, thus greater control over sensitive legal texts in contrast to proprietary systems [37,38]. Across these deployment settings, the model coverage spans dense and mixture-of-experts architectures and wide range of parameter scales. Beyond the general-purpose families, we include SteuerLLM [39], German tax-law adapted model, to examine whether legal-domain adaptation transfers to public-law examination tasks, and two European models trained outside the major vendor families: the multilingual EuroLLM [40] and Soofi-S-Isar [41], German sovereign-AI consortium release. The main evaluation set contains 32 models: 29 from nine general-purpose developer families, together with SteuerLLM, EuroLLM and Soofi-S-Isar. Twentyfive are open-weight releases, all with published parameter counts ranging from 3B to 685B; the remaining seven are proprietary hosted systems whose providers disclose none. Generation Without and With Statute Retrieval We evaluate two generation conditions over the same case facts: all 32 models without retrieval, and subset of seven of them, chosen for cost reasons, with retrieval; the prompts are reproduced in Section A.2. The conditions differ in whether statutory text is inserted into the instructions context slot and, as consequence, in the instruction that frames that slot (Section 3.3.1). Except in the oracle condition described below, no material derived from the reference solution is available during generation. Generation without retrieval. Each model receives the fixed German essay instruction and the facts of one case, and generates complete legal opinion (Gutachten). No statutory text or other external legal material is supplied. Every model receives the same 81 cases under this condition; the few essays that came back empty, truncated or errored are reported in Section 4.1. Generation with statute retrieval. For cost reasons, this condition is run on subset of seven of the 32 models  (Table 8)  . They receive the same case facts with statutory text inserted into the instructions context slot, retrieved automatically from corpus of German federal and Bavarian law. Section 3.6 describes that corpus, the retrieval pipeline and the arms we vary; Section 4.3 reports what they achieve. Across both conditions, we set no additional output-token limit, and we do not set temperature or top-p: each request uses the serving endpoints own defaults, which are recorded in the run records where the endpoint reports them (Section 3.3.3). If response contains reasoning trace delimited by <think> tags, the trace is removed before the answer is scored. 3.6. Statute Corpus and Retrieval Pipeline The retrieval task in GPBam has built-in evaluation set through the norms cited in the case solution. This lets us gauge retrieval quality independently of the final essay quality, and therefore ablate on the integration and generation aspect separately from the search itself. That opportunity is why statutory text is the primary context throughout; secondary sources enter as second knowledge source, evaluated both as context in their own right and as route to the statutes they cite. Corpus. German public law lies at the intersection of federal regulations and respective state law, with applicability crucial part of the legal appraisal. We therefore construct combined corpus of federal law from the gesetze-im-internet dump maintained by the QuantLaw project [67],6 parsed into 106,354 provisions across 5,936 law books, and of Bavarian state law collected from BAYERN.RECHT, the portal of the Bayerische Staatskanzlei [68], comprising all 7,008 available provisions from 720 statutes. The combined index holds 113,362 provisions. Both halves are built the same way: we extract the provision text, chunk at law-paragraph borders, and fold the law metadata (name, law book, paragraph) into the indexed text. The federal dump contains no Landesrecht at all, and 38.7% of the distinct norms reference solution cites are exactly that, so federal-only corpus caps recall at 54.2% against the combined corpuss 91.3%  (Table 6)  . As an additional knowledge source we index Leitsätze, headnotes produced over legal decisions by German legal publisher as secondary literature. Headnotes are short - 306 characters and 40 words on the mean, 285 characters at the median - but they carry explicit guidance on how the law was applied and summarise the decision at the same time. We index 38,966 of them, extracted from the German legal decision corpus of Urchs et al. [69] and covering the Bavarian public-law courts over 20152020. Each carries the Normenkette of its decision, 6branch data, revision 67e0567, scrape dated 2026-02-09 which is what makes second hop to statutes possible. Roughly 4% are amtliche headnotes written by the court itself, the remainder editorial work by legal publisher. Query construction. Before generation, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B rewrites each case into three to five stand-alone legal concepts or questions, an implicit query diversification scheme. This moves some of the legal knowledge boundary onto the rewriter, but both previous retrieval studies [18,19] and our own find that it clearly outperforms other rewriting strategies as well as the raw task description (tripling gold-norm recall@50 against the raw case text). The concept rewrites are generated once and reused across every arm that searches, so that two search arms differ in the retrieval component under study and not in the query. Search and fusion. For dense retrieval, we use LanceDBs Sentence Transformers [70] integration with jina-embeddings-v5-text-small-retrieval, tasktargeted distillation of the Jina v5 text family [71]. We retain the adapters default encoding behaviour for both corpus indexing and query embedding and combine this dense channel with lexical BM25 [21] retrieval over the same corpus. For each rewritten query, reciprocal rank fusion (RRF; kRRF=60) [20] first merges the dense and BM25 rankings. RRF is then applied second time across the resulting rankings from all rewritten queries. The ten highest-ranked passages are passed to the generator unless different passage budget is specified. In short, the two retrieval methods produce candidate rankings for each rewritten query, and RRF is applied twice: first to merge the dense and BM25 rankings within each query, and then to merge the results across the rewritten queries before the highest-ranked passages are passed to the generator. Retrieval arms The retrieval arms vary passage budget and components  (Table 8)  . The cite arms resolve norms named by separate rewriter; cite-only provides them alone, while cite+RRF fills the remaining budget with hybrid search. Other arms re-rank with Qwen3-Reranker-4B [72], resolve the Normenketten of twenty retrieved headnotes, or supply headnotes directly. Finally, an oracle supplies the full text of provisions cited by the solution. It bounds corpus retrieval and is not deployable. 3.7. LLM Judge Ensemble Complete legal case solutions are open-ended: legally adequate answers may differ substantially in wording while expressing equivalent legal analyses. Consequently, lexical or shallow semantic similarity to reference solution cannot by itself assess issue spotting, doctrinal assessment, completeness, structure, or subsumption. At benchmark scale, manual assessment of such responses requires costly annotation by legal experts [12,5]. Recent legal benchmarks therefore employ rubricor reference-guided LLM judges as scalable semantic evaluators. Comparisons with expert annotation show that carefully specified judges can provide useful assessments [6,5,4]. These studies also identify differences in judge severity, prompt sensitivity, and model-family preference [33,5,4,32]. Each essay is therefore graded independently by three open-weight LLM judges drawn from three different developers: GPT-oss-120b, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, and DeepSeek-V4-Flash. Panels of this kind have been reported to grade legal answers more reliably than their strongest single member: on German examination scripts, as shown by [35], pooling three models raises agreement with expert marks by up to 0.15 QWK over the best member when the full grading context is supplied, and an ensemble judge is also what LEXam validates against expert assessment [6]. The composition additionally reduces dependence on any single evaluator and limits the influence of developer or model-specific evaluation preferences. Because judges may nevertheless differ systematically in severity, we aggregate their essay-level scores using the median. With three judges, the median retains the central assessment while limiting the influence of one atypically high or low score. We report absolute and rank agreement between the seats at essay and model level in Section 5.1. All judges receive the same evidence in the prompt: the case, its reference solution, and the generated essay. The instructions guide each judge to align the reference and generated answers by section and assess correctness, completeness, legal reasoning, structure, depth of subsumption, and statutory citations, scoring how far the essay matches the solutions results, subsumption, and citations, and crediting deviations from the solution only if they are legally sound. Each judge is instructed to return score from 0.0 to 1.0 in increments of 0.1. The complete judge prompt is reproduced in Section A.2.4. To anchor the judge scale, we additionally submit three controls for each case: its reference solution, another cases reference solution, and an answer that repeats the case facts (Section 4.1). 3.8. Regressing Opus5 on the panel median gives slope of 0.56: the two agree almost exactly at the bottom of the range and diverge as the panels score rises. The written verdicts locate the disagreement in fabricated norms and inverted results, which the panel appears to penalise less than stronger judge does, rather than style - and that is the region the benchmarks spread lives in. We report this as bound on where the panel is most likely to be wrong, not as validation. Opus-5 is one more judge with its own strictness prior, and no human grades exist for GPBam. 6. Discussion & Conclusion We build GPBam to answer what short-answer legal benchmarks cannot: When model fails to write Gutachten, is it because it does not know the law, or because it cannot apply it? The retrieval ladder answers that by supplying the law and we find that the law helps, by real but bounded amount. Supplying the statute helps, but closes no gap. An oracle supplying the provisions the solution cites is worth 26 points across the seven generators  (Table 8)  ; handed that 91.3%, no generator cites even half of what it is given (41.4% at best). Retrieval gains lag far behind recall. Gold-norm recall varies roughly threefold across our configurations while essay score moves by at most 4.1 points, and the oracles 91.31% buys at most 3.3 more points over RAG. How those norms are packaged matters far less consistently: padding, reordering and ten-norm subset each cost some generators much of the gain and others almost none  (Table 10)  . That bears directly on work that evaluates the retrieval step in isolation [7]: for these generators, pipeline can be made much better at finding the right norms without becoming better at the task the norms are for. The rewriters memory outranks the search channel. Naming the provisions and resolving them by exact key no search at all beats hybrid search on goldnorm recall, but not on state law  (Table 8)  . One reading is that statute text is simply the wrong register to search with case: Sachverhalt raises doctrinal concepts, and statute rarely names the doctrine it embodies. However, some models reproduce statutory text better than they write legal opinions while the mid-tier proprietary systems do the reverse. Perhaps they hold the material but cannot apply it in the Gutachtenstil the examination rewards. The panel is internally consistent. Three diverse judges rank the 32 models nearidentically (ρ=0.950.99) so the ranking is not an artefact of any single seat. For our public-law cases, the difficulty of the Gutachten lies in applying law, not obtaining statutes which larger corpus cannot solve alone. 7. Limitations & Future Work Limitation. GPBam contains 81 state-exam-style public-law cases from one Bavarian preparation course; results may not generalize to official examinations, other legal domains, institutions, or jurisdictions. All essay scores come from three LLM judges, without expert grades. Their agreement measures consistency rather than validity and cannot detect shared bias. Every RAG delta also carries template change (Section 3.3.1), so none isolates retrieval from framing. The wording withheld arm bounds it at 0.19 to +0.56 across all three  (Table 10)  , including the generator with the largest retrieval gain. Claude-opus-5 alone ran with harness system prompt; transcripts show no access beyond the prompt file, but the prompt may account for part of its lead. The scores should not be read as German examination grades or used to assess students. At model level, score also correlates with answer length (ρ=0.71), and our design cannot distinguish greater completeness from preference for longer answers [74,33]. The material is held out rather than released, so results cannot be independently reproduced from the sources, except for the released retrieval task. Finally, the reported model-level correlations are descriptive and do not establish that statutory recall or citation overlap causes better legal reasoning. The corpus is Bavarian and federal only: it excludes the 1,476 Verwaltungsvorschriften and holds just 7.2% of the EU provisions the solutions cite. It holds statutes in their current version, so provision may have been amended since the reference solution was written. All three judges are also generators, though the per-case median limits bias effects. Future work. The judge panel should be validated against independent grades from qualified examiners for GPBam outputs while accounting for variation in German exam grading [30] and to establish whether the judge panel sits inside the range of human disagreement or outside it. Our retrieval findings suggest that statutes are the wrong register to search with: in our corpus, doctrinal vocabulary of the kind Sachverhalt raises (e.g. Rücksichtnahmegebot, Störerauswahl ) occurs only in 0.39% of statute passages, while 38.5% of court decisions use those terms. Leitsätze supply that missing register. Our highest-recall arm already routes through them, resolving each retrieved headnotes Normenkette rather than reading its text  (Table 8)  , so searching the court decisions behind them and integrating full commentaries are the next steps.
